title: Dating Apps Go Offline in India as Singles Tire of the Swipe
excerpt: Match Group's The League, Bumble and Tinder are betting on real-world mixers — singles runs, pickleball, curated dinners — after surveys show Indian users want conversations that outlast small talk. But veterans of the mixer circuit say the offline economy has problems of its own.
body:
• The League, Match Group's premium platform, launched in India in November 2025 with curated offline events; Bumble ran Puma-branded singles runs in Bengaluru (November 2024) and Mumbai (February 2025); Tinder hosted a Delhi pickleball mixer on February 9, 2025.
  • A YouGov survey of 500+ single dating-app users in Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru, commissioned by The League (reported August 2026): 69% say app chats rarely move beyond small talk; 90% would attend curated offline dating experiences.
  • Preferred formats: cultural events like art, theatre and film (49%), professional networking (48%), intimate dinners (46%) and creative workshops (45%); 51% want verified or screened communities.
  • The sceptics' case: a Mumbai singles-mixer veteran of 15 years says the offline economy monetises loneliness — she once paid over ₹12,000 for a dinner with three men she'd never have swiped on — and argues apps at least give women agency over who they interact with.

For a decade, dating apps sold Indian singles one promise: romance, outsourced to an algorithm. Now the apps are asking users to leave the house — and the industry's own research says a large majority are willing to go.

The pivot is visible in the events calendars. The League launched in India in November 2025 with curated offline experiences built in; Bumble ran Puma singles runs in Bengaluru and Mumbai; Tinder organised a Delhi pickleball mixer. As a column in The Hindu analysing the trend puts it, these are attempts to give singles something to do while they meet each other.

The data is striking. The YouGov survey commissioned by The League found 76% of respondents identify as high-intent daters and 57% are actively looking for a long-term partner. The problem is the medium: 74% of those with dating burnout say they feel like a number rather than a person.

Context & Background

Indian singles have been invited into rooms full of strangers before. Formats such as Mix and Mingle, Covalence and Footloose ran events as early as 2010–11, paused for the pandemic, and returned as apps grew dominant. What is new is who now organises the rooms: the apps themselves.

The shift reflects wider disillusionment. A 2024 YouGov survey found two out of three Indian app users had never met a match in person, citing fake profiles and mismatched intentions. In Bengaluru, organisers say singles are logging out of apps for in-person mixers — men exhausted by endless swiping with few matches, women overwhelmed by volume and wary of catfishers. The industry's answer is hybrid: the app for discovery, the event for connection.

The League's approach is deliberately small: 30 curated offline events across its markets, roughly 100 attendees in total. It has also tried to fix conversation itself — its "You Don't Want to Date Me (...Unless You Do)" initiative, built with self-discovery architect Akshat Rajan, uses guided prompts to push interactions past small talk.

Impact & Analysis

Whether the offline boom delivers depends on whose verdict you trust. The survey suggests the demand is for experiences first, dating second — as the columnist summarises, nobody wants a "dating event"; they want an interesting event where there happen to be single people.

"Our goal is to create the conditions for intentional connection, both on the app and beyond it."

— Anukool Kumar, Senior Director for India and the Middle East, Match Group

Shaista Vaishnav, a 43-year-old Mumbai professional who has attended mixers for 15 years, offers the counter-argument: the mixer economy has become a business built around loneliness, with intimate, premium-priced events targeting divorced and older singles willing to pay for companionship.

Her point about agency cuts deepest. On an app, a woman chooses who she interacts with; at a mixer, she can end up seated across from someone she would never have selected. For queer singles the calculus differs: Tejaswi Subramanian, digital editor at Gaysi, says queer offline spaces are "more fundamentally about community-building" — low-stakes socialisation where romance is only one possible outcome.

Diaspora Angle

The same fatigue runs through the diaspora, where singles in New York, San Francisco and Toronto report identical complaints layered over community marriage expectations. Offline South Asian singles events already draw crowds in the diaspora, and India's hybrid model may prove exportable. The diaspora's tension is sharper: a dating culture suspended between app individualism and family-mediated tradition, where a "curated" event can read as modern or suspiciously matrimonial depending on who is curating.

What's Next

The apps will not abandon the swipe — it remains the revenue engine. The realistic outcome is the hybrid model industry watchers describe: digital discovery feeding real-world experiences, with the surviving formats built around genuine activity rather than the audition-like pressure of a room labelled "singles." The contradiction to solve: people want to meet in person, but not feel they walked into an audition for someone's partner.
image_caption: Singles at a speed-dating event at a Nairobi hotel. Dating apps including Bumble and Tinder are expanding into real-world singles events in India as users report fatigue with app-based matchmaking. (Representative photo, Wikimedia Commons)
